title: File:An incomplete ceramic tile with hobnail impressions, dating to the Late Roman period. (FindID 739066).jpg

extmeta.ObjectName: An incomplete ceramic tile with hobnail impressions, dating to the Late Roman period.
extmeta.Categories: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, ESS|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (51° N, 0° E)|Hobnails
extmeta.Artist: Colchester and Ipswich Museum Service, Ben Paites, 2015-10-21 09:59:23
extmeta.ImageDescription:
An incomplete ceramic tile with hobnail impressions, dating to the Late Roman period. It is oval in shape with a light orange brown colouring. The tile is cracked and significant damage can be seen along the edges and on the back. On one side is a collection of seven circles, most likely the imprint of a hobnail boot. There is a lump of white concretion on the front, that is likely much later in date.


The tile was located clsoe to the 3rd century Roman fort of Othona at Bradwell-on-Sea, which was constructed around the time of the Carausian Revolt AD286-296. Based on this, it is assumed that the tile likely dates to the late 3rd or 4th century AD,

The tile is 2.60g weight, 103.95mm length, 77.41mm width, 23.00mm thickness

extmeta.ObjectName: Medieval decorated ceramic floor tile
extmeta.Categories: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, WMID|Tiles in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (52° N, 2° W)|Archaeological objects found in Coventry
extmeta.Artist: Birmingham Museums Trust, Tom Brindle, 2010-09-13 10:32:10
extmeta.ImageDescription:
A medieval ceramic patterned floor tile of 14th to 15th century in date. The tile is decorated with a white clay slip which has been poured into a pattern created by a wooden stamp. The tile was then fired after being sprinkled with a lead ore, which had produced a slightly uneven yellow glaze. The ceramic itself is of a solid orange red/colour and also has traces of a lead glaze on the reverse. The tile is incomplete, with approximately one quarter missing from one end. It measures 125 mm in length and 104 mm wide, although when complete it would have been square. It is 28 mm thick.

What remains of the pattern on the tile is of a five petalled rose within part of a circular band of rope ornament. Although the design is damaged, it is likely that there would have been initials to either side of this rose, probably an A and M for Ave Maria (though other initials are possible). The tile is almost certainly one of a set of nine which would together have formed a circle of rope ornament. Alternating tiles would probably have had the rose and the A.M initials, whilst the corner tiles would probably have had the sacred initials I.H.C, the abbreviation of Jesus.

Similar tiles are recorded from Maxstoke Castle in North Warwickshire and from St. John's church in Coventry (Chatwin 1940, 11), which was founded in 1344. Chatwin has suggested that the type appears to have been relatively common in Warwickshire during the 14th century (Chatwin 1940, 20). However, Eames has suggested that the design actually dates from the 15th century (Eames 1980). A medieval tile kiln is known from the Harefield Estate in Stoke, Coventry, and there is therefore a strong chance that the tile was manfactured at this site. Eames' catalogue contains a number of similar examples, all from Warwickshire, which includes examples from sites at Maxstoke Priory, Preston Deanery and Bewdley (Eames 1980, cat nos 2594-2600;2731;1399).

extmeta.ImageDescription: An incomplete fired ceramic floor tile, dating from the Medieval to the Post-Medieval period. The object is sub-rectangular in plan and rectangular in cross-section. Each edge is incomplete. The lower face of the object is sandy and uneven, due to damage. The upper face is well worn. The object has a mid-orange fabric with occasional small inclusions. The object has been fired evenly. The thickness of this fragment indicates that it is likely to have been used as a floor tile.

title: File:Medieval foor finial tile, horse's head, as broken (FindID 425214).jpg

extmeta.ObjectName: Medieval foor finial tile, horse's head, as broken
extmeta.Categories: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Figurines in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Portable Antiquities Scheme, DENO|Tiles in the Portable Antiquities Scheme|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (52° N, 2° W)
extmeta.Artist: Derby Museums Trust, Rachel Atherton, 2011-01-24 10:13:12
extmeta.ImageDescription:
Medieval pottery figurine in the form of a stylised horse's head/neck. Modelled in the round with striations indicating the mane on the neck and forehead; the head is broken away from the body but is present, although damaged at the ears, one eye and along the snout; the surviving eye is formed by an impressed ring and dot - the eye is orange coloured and appears to have been applied separately. A short applied strip on the left side of the neck, behind the mane, perhaps indicates the bridle/reins. Degraded yellow-green glaze. Coarse very sandy fabric with reduced-fired grey core and oxidised-fired skin varying cream and orange; abundant angular white quartz sand inclusions (0.5mm-3mm) giving pimply appearence to surface. In two fragments - the head is broken away from the neck. Length (from the break at the neck to the forehead) 104mm, width (throat to mane) 80mm, thickness at base of neck 35mm, weight 182.8g + 48.1g.

This is probably a fragment of a roof-finial tile, or possibly an aquamanile or other fancy pottery vessel fragment. The lack of a pouring spout through the head, and the coarseness of the fabric, perhaps preclude this from being an aquamanile / vessel.

Blair & Ramsay, 1991 ("English Medieval Industries: craftsmen, techniques, products", Continuum) write 'Finials of stone, wood or pottery were used from the 11th century onwards to decorate the gable and the ridges of medieval roofs. Some were in the form of spikes, other like human faces, and some represented standing animals such as horses, bears, dragons or lions.' They note that ceramic tililng was first used during the medieval period in England during the 12th century, and that 'the earliest archaeological and documentary evidence for ridge tiles dates from the 13th century'.

extmeta.ImageDescription: Ceramic fragment probably dating from the late medieval or post-medieval period, i.e. c. AD1500-1800. Even though it is quite thin and damaged, it may possibly have been a floor tile fragment. It was made from a light cream-coloured earthenware and it was probably glazed. However, none of the glaze survives on the sherd. It is very worn.
